title: Conduction system, cardiac cycle and blood pressure
blurb: Order the conduction pathway, read the P, QRS and T waves, and work out cardiac output and blood pressure.
question: An impulse starts in the wall of the right atrium. Which structures carry it, in order, until the ventricles contract, and what does the QRS complex on an ECG show?

teach.h: The heart sets its own beat
teach.body: Formally, cardiac muscle is autorhythmic: specialized cells generate impulses without any signal from the brain, and the conduction system spreads them in a fixed order. The autonomic nervous system only changes the rate: sympathetic nerves speed it up, parasympathetic (vagus) nerves slow it down. In plain English: the heart has its own built-in spark plug, and the nervous system just presses the gas or the brake.

steps.label: Bundle branches
steps.sub: Right and left, in the septum

teach.body: If the impulse raced straight from the atria to the ventricles, both would contract at once and the ventricles would squeeze before they had filled. The AV node holds the signal back for a moment so the atria finish emptying into the ventricles first. Ventricular contraction then starts at the apex and moves upward, pushing blood toward the exit valves at the top, like squeezing toothpaste from the bottom of the tube.

teach.caption: The fastest pacemaker sets the pace. If the SA node fails, the next one down takes over at a slower rate.
Atrial repolarization has no wave of its own: it is hidden inside the QRS complex.
Systole = contraction; diastole = relaxation and filling.

teach.body: Cardiac output (CO) is the volume pumped per minute: CO = heart rate × stroke volume. At about 72 beats/min × 70 mL, that is roughly 5 L/min, about the body's whole blood volume. Blood pressure is written systolic (during ventricular contraction) over diastolic (during relaxation); normal adult is below 120/80 mmHg. BP depends on cardiac output and peripheral resistance, set by arteriole diameter. It is measured with a sphygmomanometer, usually at the brachial artery.

Marcus, a nursing applicant, has a physical before starting his program. His heart rate is 80 beats/min and his stroke volume is estimated at 65 mL. Cardiac output = 80 × 65 = 5,200 mL/min = 5.2 L/min. His blood pressure is 116/74 mmHg: both numbers are below 120/80, so it is in the normal range. His ECG shows a P wave before every QRS complex, so each beat starts at the SA node.

teach.text: Order traps: the SA node fires BEFORE the AV node, and the bundle of His comes BEFORE the Purkinje fibers. Wave traps: P = atrial depolarization, T = ventricular repolarization. Formula trap: cardiac output = heart rate × STROKE VOLUME, not heart rate × blood pressure.

items: SA node, atria, AV node (delay), bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers, ventricles.
Backup rates: SA 60–100, AV node 40–60, ventricles 20–40 per minute.
P = atrial depolarization; QRS = ventricular depolarization; T = ventricular repolarization.
Sympathetic speeds the heart; parasympathetic (vagus) slows it.
CO = HR × SV (about 5 L/min); normal BP below 120/80 mmHg.

summary: You can now order the conduction pathway, explain the AV node delay, and match the P wave, QRS complex and T wave to their electrical events. You can also calculate cardiac output, describe the cardiac cycle and interpret a blood pressure reading.

A.q: Which structure is the heart's natural pacemaker?
A.why: The SA node, in the wall of the right atrium, fires about 60–100 times a minute and sets the normal heart rate.

whyNot.0: The AV node delays the impulse and is a slower backup (about 40–60/min), not the normal pacemaker.
whyNot.1: The bundle of His carries the impulse from the AV node into the septum; it does not start it.
whyNot.3: Purkinje fibers spread the impulse through the ventricle walls at the end of the pathway.

A.q: On an ECG, the QRS complex represents:
A.why: The QRS complex is ventricular depolarization, which triggers ventricular contraction.

whyNot.0: Atrial depolarization is the P wave.
whyNot.2: Ventricular repolarization is the T wave.
whyNot.3: Atrial repolarization is hidden inside the QRS complex but is not what the QRS represents.

A.why: Cardiac output is the volume pumped per minute: beats per minute × volume per beat (stroke volume).

whyNot.1: Blood pressure depends on cardiac output; it is not a factor in calculating it.
whyNot.2: Stroke volume must be multiplied by heart rate, not by pressure, to give volume per minute.
whyNot.3: Blood volume is the total in the body, not the amount pumped per beat.

B.q: What is the main purpose of the brief delay at the AV node?
options: Lets the atria refill before contracting
Lets the SA node reset before the next beat
Lets the semilunar valves open fully first
Lets the ventricles fill before contracting
B.why: The AV node delay gives the atria time to finish emptying, so the ventricles are full before they contract.

whyNot.0: The atria refill during diastole; the AV delay is about the ventricles filling.
whyNot.1: The SA node fires on its own rhythm; the AV delay is not for resetting it.
whyNot.2: Semilunar valves open when the ventricles contract, after the delay, not because of it.

B.q: If the SA node stops firing, the AV node can take over as pacemaker at about:
B.why: The AV node's intrinsic rate is about 40–60 beats/min, slower than the SA node.

whyNot.1: 60–100 beats/min is the SA node's normal rate.
whyNot.2: 20–40 beats/min is the ventricles' own backup rate, the slowest.
whyNot.3: 100–120 beats/min is faster than any built-in backup pacemaker.

B.q: Stimulation of the vagus (parasympathetic) nerve to the heart would most likely:
options: Shift the pacemaker to the AV node
B.why: Parasympathetic (vagus) stimulation slows the heart rate; the autonomic system changes the rate but does not create the beat.

whyNot.0: Speeding up the heart is the sympathetic system's effect.
whyNot.1: The SA node stays the pacemaker; the vagus just slows its firing.
whyNot.3: Cardiac muscle stays autorhythmic; nerves only adjust the rate.

C.q: A patient has a heart rate of 75 beats/min and a stroke volume of 68 mL. What is the cardiac output?
C.why: CO = HR × SV = 75 × 68 = 5,100 mL/min. Dividing by 1,000 gives 5.1 L/min.

whyNot.0: 51 L/min comes from dividing 5,100 mL by 100 instead of 1,000.
whyNot.2: 0.51 L/min comes from dividing 5,100 mL by 10,000 instead of 1,000.
whyNot.3: 1.1 comes from dividing 75 by 68 instead of multiplying.

C.q: In the conduction pathway, which structure receives the impulse immediately after the bundle of His?
C.why: The bundle of His (AV bundle) divides into the right and left bundle branches in the septum, which then feed the Purkinje fibers.

whyNot.0: Purkinje fibers come AFTER the bundle branches.
whyNot.1: The AV node comes BEFORE the bundle of His.
whyNot.2: The apex is where contraction begins once the Purkinje fibers deliver the impulse, two steps later.

C.q: During a pre-admission physical, Hannah's blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg. Which statement is correct?
options: The systolic value is above the normal limit
The diastolic value is above the normal limit
Both values are within the normal range
The systolic value reflects ventricular relaxation
C.why: Normal adult BP is below 120 systolic and below 80 diastolic. 128 is above 120, while 78 is below 80.

whyNot.1: The diastolic value, 78, is below 80, so it is within the normal range.
whyNot.2: The systolic value, 128, is above the normal limit of 120.
whyNot.3: Systolic pressure is measured during ventricular CONTRACTION; diastolic reflects relaxation.

reteach.title: A relay race with a planned pause
reteach.question: Think of a relay race where one handoff deliberately waits a moment. How does that match the path of an impulse through the heart?

blocks.body: The SA node fires the starting gun and the first runner sprints across the atria, which contract. At the AV node the baton is held for a moment: this planned pause lets the ventricles fill. Then the baton flies down the bundle of His, splits into the right and left bundle branches, and the Purkinje fibers carry it to every part of the ventricle walls, which squeeze from the bottom up.

blocks.text: The race always starts at the SA node, never the AV node, and the split lanes (bundle branches) come before the finish (Purkinje fibers).

explain.body: SA node (pacemaker in the RA wall), atria contract, AV node (delay), AV bundle (bundle of His), bundle branches in the septum, Purkinje fibers, ventricles contract from the apex upward.

test.q: Which sequence of the conduction system is correct?
options: AV node, SA node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
SA node, AV node, Purkinje fibers, bundle of His
SA node, AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
SA node, bundle of His, AV node, Purkinje fibers
test.why: The impulse goes SA node, AV node, bundle of His, then (via the bundle branches) the Purkinje fibers.

whyNot.0: The SA node fires first; the AV node comes second.
whyNot.1: The bundle of His comes before the Purkinje fibers.
whyNot.3: The AV node comes before the bundle of His, which carries the impulse on from it.

explain.body: P wave: atrial depolarization. QRS complex: ventricular depolarization (atrial repolarization is hidden inside it). T wave: ventricular repolarization.

test.q: On an ECG, the T wave represents:
test.why: The T wave shows the ventricles repolarizing (recovering) after contraction.

whyNot.0: Atrial repolarization is hidden inside the QRS complex.
whyNot.2: Ventricular depolarization is the QRS complex.
whyNot.3: Atrial depolarization is the P wave.

explain.body: Systole is contraction; diastole is relaxation and filling. The autonomic nervous system changes the rate only: sympathetic speeds it up, parasympathetic (vagus) slows it down.

test.q: In the cardiac cycle, the term diastole refers to:
options: The pause at the AV node
The moment the AV valves close
test.why: Diastole is the relaxation phase, when a chamber fills with blood.

whyNot.1: The AV node delay is an electrical event, not a phase of the cycle.
whyNot.2: AV valve closure (S1) marks the start of ventricular systole, not diastole.

explain.body: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume (about 5 L/min). Blood pressure = systolic over diastolic; normal adult below 120/80 mmHg. BP depends on cardiac output and peripheral resistance, which arterioles set by constricting or dilating.

test.q: Which change would most directly raise blood pressure?
test.why: Narrowing arterioles raises peripheral resistance, which raises blood pressure.

whyNot.1: Vasodilation lowers resistance, so blood pressure falls.
whyNot.2: A smaller stroke volume lowers cardiac output, so pressure falls.
whyNot.3: A slower heart rate lowers cardiac output, so pressure falls.
